usage: Counting small candies with 하나/한 개 is the most natural way at a register.
Drop the subject in casual talk; context makes 'you' clear.
막대(stick) + 사탕 — a fixed compound, written as one word.
Want me to unwrap the candy for you?
까다 (to peel/unwrap) is the everyday verb for opening wrapped candy.
examples: 편의점에서 사탕 한 봉지 샀어요.
I bought a bag of candy at the convenience store.
봉지 is the counter for a bag/packet of snacks.
목 아플 때 사탕 하나 먹으면 좀 나아요.
When my throat hurts, eating a candy helps a bit.
Many Koreans treat throat-soothing candy as a mild remedy.
애들이 사탕만 먹으려고 해서 걱정이에요.
The kids only want to eat candy, so I'm worried.
만 = 'only'; 먹으려고 하다 = 'try/want to eat'.
nuance: 사탕 covers hard candy and lollipops, not gummies (those are 젤리) or chocolate (초콜릿). On Valentine's Day women give 초콜릿, and on White Day (March 14) men reciprocate with 사탕, so the word carries a small romantic-gift nuance in season.
mistakes: Calling gummy candies 사탕 — soft chewy ones are 젤리, not 사탕.
Saying 사탕을 열다 to mean 'unwrap a candy'; Koreans say 사탕을 까다.

usage: 개 counts individual pieces; 판 counts a whole bar.
녹다 (to melt) is the verb you'll hear in summer.
Loanword modifiers like 다크/밀크 sit directly before 초콜릿.
Cut back on chocolate a little
줄이다 = to reduce; common health-talk phrasing.
examples: 밸런타인데이에 친구한테 초콜릿 줬어요.
I gave my friend chocolate on Valentine's Day.
Giving 초콜릿 on Feb 14 is a big custom in Korea.
피곤할 때 초콜릿 먹으면 기분이 좀 좋아져요.
When I'm tired, eating chocolate lifts my mood a bit.
기분이 좋아지다 = one's mood improves.
이 빵 안에 초콜릿이 들어 있어요.
There's chocolate inside this bread.
들어 있다 = to be contained inside.
nuance: Note the spelling: 초콜릿, not 초콜렛 (a very common misspelling even among natives). The standard counter for a bar is 판, while individual squares or pieces use 개. Chocolate is the default Valentine's gift from women to men, mirrored by 사탕 on White Day.
mistakes: Writing 초콜렛 instead of the standard 초콜릿.
Using 판 for a single piece — a whole bar is 한 판, one square is 한 개.

usage: Sold by the 봉지 at convenience stores.
곰(bear) + 젤리; the most popular type by far.
쫄깃하다 describes the springy chew people love.
Casual permission with -아/어도 돼요? shortened to 돼?
examples: 요즘 마라맛 젤리 같은 신기한 맛도 많아요.
These days there are even unusual flavors like mala gummies.
마라맛 (mala flavor) is a recent trend; 신기하다 = novel/curious.
젤리는 충치 생기기 쉬우니까 조금만 먹어.
Gummies cause cavities easily, so eat just a little.
생기기 쉽다 = easy to develop; 조금만 = just a little.
편의점 젤리 코너 앞에서 한참 골랐어요.
I spent ages choosing in front of the gummy section at the convenience store.
한참 = a good while; 고르다 = to pick.
nuance: 젤리 is the catch-all for chewy gummies (gummy bears, fruit gummies), distinct from hard 사탕. It also names wobbly dessert jellies, but in everyday snack talk it almost always means gummies. Convenience stores in Korea carry an enormous, frequently rotating gummy selection, so it's a high-frequency word.
mistakes: Confusing 젤리 (gummy) with 잼 (jam/spread) — different foods entirely.
Calling 젤리 a kind of 사탕; Koreans keep the two categories separate.

usage: 봉지 is the go-to counter for bagged snacks.
부스러기 = crumbs; useful when cleaning up.
눅눅하다 describes chips that lost their crunch.
-(으)러 가다 = go to do; 갈래? is a casual invite.
examples: 영화 볼 때 과자랑 음료수는 필수예요.
Snacks and a drink are a must when watching a movie.
필수예요 = it's essential/a must.
이 과자 한번 먹으면 손을 못 멈춰요.
Once you start this snack, you can't stop your hand.
손을 못 멈추다 = can't stop (eating); playful exaggeration.
과자 봉지가 생각보다 절반이 공기예요.
Half the snack bag is air, more than you'd think.
A common joke about 질소과자 (nitrogen-filled bags).
nuance: 과자 is the umbrella term for crunchy packaged snacks — chips, crackers, biscuits, corn snacks — basically the salty/sweet bagged stuff in the snack aisle. It does not cover gummies (젤리), candy (사탕), or chocolate. Koreans joke about 질소과자, bags that feel mostly full of nitrogen gas rather than chips.
mistakes: Using 과자 for cookies you'd call 쿠키 in a cafe — 과자 leans toward packaged/mass-market snacks.
Treating 과자 as countable by piece; bagged snacks are counted by 봉지.

usage: 통 (tub/bucket) is the cinema counter for popcorn.
Flavor sits before 팝콘; 카라멜/치즈 are most common.
튀기다 (to fry/pop) is the standard verb.
Cinemas let you split flavors; 반반 = half-half.
examples: 영화관에서 팝콘 큰 거 하나 시켰어요.
I ordered one large popcorn at the cinema.
큰 거 = the big one; 시키다 = to order.
고소한 팝콘 냄새 때문에 안 사고는 못 배겨요.
The savory popcorn smell makes it impossible not to buy some.
고소하다 = nutty/savory; idiomatic 못 배기다 = can't resist.
집에서 전자레인지 팝콘 돌려 먹었어요.
I made microwave popcorn at home.
돌리다 = to run (the microwave), then 먹다.
nuance: 팝콘 is strongly tied to the cinema in Korea, where caramel and cheese (and half-and-half, 반반) are the default choices, often bundled with a drink in a 콤보 set. The cinema counter is 통, while microwave popcorn at home uses 봉지. The smell is classic 고소하다 (savory-nutty).
mistakes: Ordering popcorn by 개 — at a cinema you ask for 한 통 (one tub).
Forgetting that flavored popcorn is the norm; plain butter is less common than caramel/cheese.

usage: 개 also works; 하나 is the easy default at a stall.
Drop the verb at a busy stall; 개 + 요 is enough.
examples: 겨울에 길거리에서 따뜻한 호떡 먹는 게 최고예요.
Eating warm hotteok on the street in winter is the best.
Hotteok is a quintessential winter street food; -는 게 최고예요 = is the best.
호떡 안에 흑설탕이 흘러나와서 입천장 데었어요.
The brown sugar oozed out of the hotteok and I burned the roof of my mouth.
흑설탕 = brown sugar; the molten filling is famously hot.
호떡 한 입 베어 물자마자 너무 뜨거웠어요.
The moment I bit into the hotteok it was way too hot.
베어 물다 = to bite into; -자마자 = as soon as.
nuance: 호떡 is a chewy griddle-fried pancake with a molten brown-sugar-and-cinnamon center, sold piping hot from winter street carts. The filling is dangerously hot, so locals warn 천천히 먹어 (eat slowly). Trendy versions like 씨앗 호떡 (packed with seeds and nuts) are popular in markets like Busan's BIFF square.
mistakes: Expecting 호떡 to be savory — the classic filling is sweet brown sugar.
Confusing 호떡 with 떡 (rice cake); 호떡 is a wheat-flour pancake, not made of 떡.

usage: Sold in counts; often cheaper as a 묶음 (bundle).
슈크림 fillings now rival the classic 팥(red bean).
Do you eat the head or tail first?
A playful national debate; both are fine.
examples: 요즘은 붕어빵 파는 데 찾기가 힘들어요.
These days it's hard to find a place selling bungeoppang.
Stalls have become scarce; there's even a 붕어빵 지도 app.
붕어빵은 팥이 꼬리까지 꽉 차 있어야 진짜죠.
A real bungeoppang has red bean packed all the way to the tail.
꽉 차다 = packed full; locals judge stalls by this.
추운 날 붕어빵 봉지 들고 호호 불면서 먹었어요.
On a cold day I ate bungeoppang from the bag, blowing on it.
호호 불다 = to blow (to cool); cozy winter image.
nuance: 붕어빵 is a fish-shaped waffle-batter pastry filled with sweet red-bean paste, the iconic Korean winter street snack alongside 호떡 and 군고구마. Custard (슈크림) and pizza fillings now compete with the classic 팥. Stalls have grown rare enough that fans share locations via a 'bungeoppang map' app, and locals fondly debate eating head-first vs. tail-first.
mistakes: Thinking 붕어빵 contains fish — it's named only for its fish shape; the classic filling is red bean.
Counting it with 마리 (the animal counter); use 개 for the pastry.

usage: Sold by the piece (개) or by weight.
Is the roasted sweet potato warm?
Warmth is the whole point in winter.
Peel the skin off and eat it
꿀고구마 = an extra-sweet, moist variety people request.
examples: 겨울 되니까 군고구마 생각이 간절해요.
Now that it's winter, I really crave roasted sweet potato.
생각이 간절하다 = to crave intensely.
요즘은 편의점에서도 군고구마를 팔더라고요.
These days they even sell roasted sweet potatoes at convenience stores.
-더라고요 reports a surprising observation.
군고구마는 호일에 싸여 있어서 손이 안 뜨거워요.
The roasted sweet potato is wrapped in foil so your hands don't get hot.
호일에 싸이다 = to be wrapped in foil.
nuance: 군고구마 (구운 + 고구마, 'roasted sweet potato') is a beloved winter street snack, traditionally sold from a barrel-drum roaster on a cart and now also stocked warm at convenience stores. People prize the 꿀고구마 type for its sticky, honey-like sweetness. It pairs in the winter trio with 호떡 and 붕어빵.
mistakes: Saying 구운 고구마 when ordering — the fixed compound 군고구마 is what's used as a name.
Confusing 고구마 (sweet potato) with 감자 (potato); they're different vegetables.

usage: Sold by 인분 (portion) at 분식 stalls.
Dip it in salt to eat
Many eat 순대 with salt; 찍다 = to dip.
Do you eat the organ meats too?
내장 (liver, lung) comes mixed in; some skip it.
Dip the sundae in the tteokbokki sauce
examples: 분식집에서 순대랑 튀김 같이 시켰어요.
I ordered sundae and fritters together at the snack shop.
분식집 = snack/street-food shop; 같이 시키다 = order together.
순대는 소금이랑 먹을지 양념장이랑 먹을지 늘 고민돼요.
I always agonize over eating sundae with salt or with seasoned sauce.
양념장 = seasoned sauce; regional preferences differ.
아바이 순대는 일반 순대보다 훨씬 커요.
Abai sundae is much bigger than regular sundae.
아바이순대 is a famous Sokcho specialty.
nuance: 순대 is a steamed sausage of pig intestine stuffed with 당면 (glass noodles) and other fillings, a staple of 분식 (snack-shop) culture alongside 떡볶이 and 튀김. There's a real regional split on whether to dip it in plain salt or 양념장. Note: the dessert spelled 'sundae' in English is unrelated — that's 선데이/아이스크림 in Korean.
mistakes: Confusing 순대 with an ice-cream sundae; the Korean snack is a savory blood sausage.
Ordering by 개 — 순대 is typically sold by 인분 (portion).

usage: 꼬치 = skewer; the street form is on a stick.
The hot 국물 (broth) is free and beloved in winter.
오뎅 is the common (Japanese-origin) colloquial term.
셀프 = self-service; refill your own paper cup.
examples: 추운 날 포장마차에서 어묵 국물 마시면 몸이 녹아요.
Drinking fish-cake broth at a street stall on a cold day warms you up.
포장마차 = street food tent; 몸이 녹다 = to thaw/warm up.
어묵 꼬치 다섯 개 먹고 국물도 두 컵 마셨어요.
I ate five fish-cake skewers and drank two cups of broth too.
Counting 꼬치 (skewers) and 컵 (cups).
부산 어묵이 유명해서 선물로 많이 사 가요.
Busan fish cake is famous, so people buy lots as gifts.
부산어묵 is a well-known regional brand/specialty.
nuance: 어묵 is the standard word for fish cake, eaten street-style on skewers (꼬치) with a free, endlessly refilled hot 국물 in winter. Many speakers casually call it 오뎅 from Japanese, though 어묵 is the 'proper' term. Busan (부산어묵) is the famous home of it, and packaged versions are common gifts and soup ingredients.
mistakes: Assuming 오뎅 is wrong — it's extremely common in speech, just not the standard term.
Forgetting the broth is self-serve and refillable; you don't pay per cup.

usage: 모둠 = an assortment of mixed pieces.
Ingredient + 튀김 names each fritter; 오징어/새우/고구마.
바삭하다 = crispy; the key quality marker.
Dip the fritters in the tteokbokki sauce
Quintessential 분식 way to eat them.
examples: 분식집에서 튀김이랑 순대 시켜서 나눠 먹었어요.
We ordered fritters and sundae at the snack shop and shared.
나눠 먹다 = to share food.
갓 튀긴 튀김이 제일 바삭하고 맛있어요.
Freshly fried fritters are the crispiest and tastiest.
갓 튀기다 = just-fried; freshness is everything.
김말이 튀김은 안에 당면이 들어 있어요.
Gimmari fritters have glass noodles inside.
김말이 = seaweed-rolled fritter, a popular type.
nuance: 튀김 means deep-fried, battered snacks in the Korean tempura tradition — fried squid, shrimp, sweet potato, and 김말이 (seaweed-noodle rolls) — sold at 분식 stalls next to 떡볶이 and 순대. The defining quality is 바삭함 (crispiness), best when 갓 튀긴 (just fried). Dipping them in spicy tteokbokki sauce is the classic move.
mistakes: Using the verb 튀기다 (to fry) when you mean the noun 튀김 (the fried food).
Expecting one item — 튀김 usually refers to an assortment; specify the ingredient (오징어 튀김 etc.) to order one kind.

usage: Counted by 개; offered with tea.
It's a honey-soaked sweet; 달다 = sweet.
Bite-size 미니 약과 became a huge trend snack.
I bought a bag of yakgwa
Packaged mini versions sell by the 봉지.
examples: 요즘 젊은 사람들 사이에서 약과가 다시 유행이에요.
Yakgwa is trendy again among young people these days.
Part of the recent '할매니얼' (grandma + millennial) retro-snack craze.
약과는 명절에 차례상에 꼭 올라가는 한과예요.
Yakgwa is a traditional sweet that always goes on the holiday ritual table.
한과 = traditional confection; 차례상 = ancestral-rite table.
약과가 겉은 쫀득하고 안은 부드러워요.
Yakgwa is chewy outside and soft inside.
쫀득하다 = pleasantly chewy/sticky.
nuance: 약과 is a traditional Korean confection (한과): wheat-flour dough fried and soaked in honey or grain syrup, historically a holiday and ritual-table sweet. It has surged back into fashion among 20-30s as part of the '할매니얼' retro-snack trend, with cafes selling 미니 약과 and yakgwa-topped desserts. It's quite sweet and pleasantly chewy (쫀득하다).
mistakes: Assuming 약과 contains medicine because of 약(藥) — the name is historical; it's just a honey cookie.
Grouping it with Western 과자 — 약과 is specifically a 한과 (traditional confection).
